newsitem.title: USA: US House approves ban on desecrating flag.
newsitem.headline: US House approves ban on desecrating flag.

text.p: Two days before Flag Day, the House Thursday approved a constitutional amendment to ban desecration of the American flag.

The measure, which needs two-thirds majorities in both the House and Senate, passed its first major hurdle on a 310-114 vote. But the Republican-backed amendment faced tougher sledding in the Senate, where Utah Republican Orrin Hatch planned to introduce it.
If it gets through both houses of Congress, the amendment would have to be ratified by 38 of the 50 states. The president's signature is not needed to amend the Constitution.

Backers said states should have an opportunity to decide the issue after a 1989 Supreme Court decision that struck down state laws against flag burning and desecration. Legislatures of 49 states -- all but Vermont -- have passed resolutions calling for an amendment.
But opponents said the measure would infringe on existing First Amendment guarantees of freedom of speech and would be used to crack down on political dissent.

"Those with contrary opinions should be free to express their opinions. Popular speech does not need protection," Representative Robert Scott, a Virginia Democrat, said. "The idea of jailing political dissidents is obviously inconsistent with our idea of freedom."

But sponsor Representative Gerald Solomon, a New York Republican, said polls showed some 80 percent of the public want a law to protect the flag. "The majority of Americans do not view flag-burning as a protected right," Solomon said.

"This in no way contradicts or weakens the First Amendment's guarantee of freedom of speech. There have always been some limitations on freedom of speech," said Illinois Republican Representative William Lipinski, another sponsor.

Democrats accused Republicans of being too eager to amend the Constitution and said this would mark the first change in the nation's history to the Bill of Rights -- the first 10 amendments, added shortly after the Constitution was drafted.
"Are we going to ... change the Constitution and amend it back when you are out of the majority?" North Carolina Democratic Representative Melvin Watt asked.

"Jefferson realised that the only way to defend the freedom of good men is to defend the freedom of all men," said Representative Wayne Gilchrest, a Maryland Republican who opposed the bill. "The House seems to value the work of Betsy Ross above the work of Madison and Jefferson."
